table.text: The studies received ethics approval from the Institutional Review Board of the Paris School of Economics (Application No. 2025-032), approved June 21, 2025.
It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others' points, knew their partner's points, or knew the group's point distribution.
In each round participants were randomly paired with three other members of their microsociety.
Participants were adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via the online research platform Prolific.
The study took approximately 15-20 minutes, and participants were paid at a rate of £9 per hour plus the bonus payment earned during the game.
Participants completed the experiment in groups of eight, with each group assigned to one of the four conditions.

The Threshold treatment determined the points level below which participants were penalised: 200 points in the Threshold conditions (a level below which participants could reasonably expect to fall) and 20 points in the No Threshold conditions (a level low enough that falling below was extremely unlikely to occur, which still preserved a formal penalty structure and equivalent complexity of instructions).
Participants completed eight rounds of the game.
In each round, participants were randomly paired with another member of their group, yielding four partner pairs.
After choosing and reporting what they expected their partner to choose, participants were shown their own choice, their partner's choice, and how their own points had changed (or remained the same).
Throughout, participants were shown a visual of their own points level relative to the threshold and the number of strikes they had incurred.

Follow-up simple contrasts found that, within the Threshold treatment level, Unequal participants had significantly greater odds of stealing than Equal participants, OR = 6.92, 95% CI [3.31, 14.49], z = 5.14, p < .001.

table.text: Crucially, we observed inequality's effects-more stealing, lower trust, less cooperation-without inequality ever being perceived, since no participant ever knew how many points any other participant had.
Participants were again adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific.

In study 1, participants were substantially more likely to steal when their resources fell below the desperation threshold (primary effect), participants who had been stolen from trusted subsequent partners less, and this mistrust in turn predicted participants' own cooperation (secondary effect).
Participants had no information about the resource levels of others, demonstrating that inequality can increase crime, reduce trust, and lower cooperation even when it is entirely unobserved.

We also tested the additional effect of inequality visibility by adding two conditions; one in which participants were informed of the resource level of their partner, one in which they were informed of the distribution of resources in the group.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via the online research platform Prolific. We determined our target sample size via a simulation-based power analysis targeting 80% power (β = .80) to detect the Threshold × Starting Points interaction. This was based on Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4 and determined to be 512 participants (approximately 64 groups of 8, 16 groups per treatment condition, 128 participants per condition). The final sample for Study 1, after exclusions, included 496 participants and 3,661 observations (64 groups; M age = 42.6, SD = 13.0, range = 18-81; 53% female, 46% male, 1% unreported). The study took approximately 15-20 minutes, and participants were paid at a rate of £9 per hour plus the bonus payment earned during the game. Data collection was paused once the target sample size had completed the study. As pre-registered, participants who dropped out mid-game were replaced by bots, and additional groups were run as needed to reach the minimum required sample per condition. Participants who either ended three consecutive rounds below the threshold or who failed to respond within the choice-page time limit were replaced by bots in subsequent rounds. Bots followed a choice protocol designed to approximate the participant's prior choices when possible, and to select Work Alone when not. Bots made 307 of all choice decisions (7.7%), and these decisions were excluded from analyses. Participants' choices were included if they chose in at least three rounds; for participants replaced before three rounds, both their choices and all subsequent bot choices were excluded. See Supplementary Materials S2, for more detail.

Participants were again adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific. We determined our target sample size via a simulation-based power analysis using data from study 1, targeting 80% power (β = .80) to detect the Threshold × Starting Points interaction. This was determined to be 1,056 participants (approximately 132 groups of eight, 88 participants per treatment cell). The final sample for Study 2, after exclusions, included 1,014 participants and 7,419 observations (132 groups; M age = 38.9, SD = 12.4, range = 18-84; 58% female, 40% male, 2% unreported). The same data collection and bot replacement rules were implemented as used in study 1. Bots made 693 of all choice decisions (8.5%), and again all analyses excluded these decisions.

We determined our target sample size via a simulation-based power analysis using data from Study 4 of Radkani et al. (2023), targeting 80% power (β = .80) to detect the Threshold × Unequal Starting Points interaction. We generated balanced sub-samples for each candidate sample size (160 to 544, in steps of 32), ran 1,500 simulations per candidate size, and calculated empirical power as the proportion of simulations in which the interaction reached significance at p < .05. From our initial sample, one group had more than 2 dropouts (3 players who timed out during gameplay); as pre-registered, this group was dropped and replaced with a new group, leaving 512 participants across 64 groups (16 groups per treatment condition). All remaining groups had 2 or fewer players who dropped before round 3. We then excluded participants who completed fewer than 3 rounds of gameplay, leaving 498 participants across 64 groups, and removed all bot-generated observations. This left a final analytic sample of 496 participants across 64 groups (16 groups per treatment condition), or 3,661 round-level observations.
table.header: Study 1: Sample Size and Data Exclusion

table.text: We determined our target sample size of 1,056 participants (approximately 132 groups of eight, 88 participants per treatment cell) via a simulation-based power analysis using data from Study 1. For each candidate sample size, ranging from 160 to 480 in steps of 32, and for each of our three focal interaction predictions (P2, P4, P8), we generated 1,500 simulated balanced sub-samples and tested for a significant Threshold × Unequal Starting Points interaction in each.
table.header: Study 2: Sample Size and Data Exclusion

table.text: Empirical power at a given sample size was estimated as the proportion of simulations in which that interaction reached significance at p < .05. We selected the smallest candidate sample size giving at least 80% power across these three predictions and scaled it up to the full 2 × 2 × 3 design. The achieved sample reached the group-level target exactly-132 groups-but fell 42 participants short of the participant-level target: 1,014 participants across those 132 groups (7,419 round-level choices after exclusions), or 96.0% of the 1,056 target. This shortfall was due to 42 participant-level timeouts spread across all twelve treatment cells (range 1-7 per cell; largest shortfall in the equal, No-Threshold, Visible-Partner cell), consistent with the pre-registered stopping rule under which timed-out participants are replaced by a bot for the remainder of the session rather than the group being re-run.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Why does Inequality Reduce Trust and Undermine Cooperation? Testing A Compositional Account
table.research_questions:
Research Question Overview

This study will test two categories of questions. First, it will aim to recover the behavioural effects found in Radkani et al. (2023) by testing the following basic predictions arising from the desperation threshold model, i.e., that when individuals are below (vs. above) a desperation threshold they should steal more (primary effect), and that exposure to stealing will both worsen individuals’ expectations of what their partner will choose (i.e., increase stealing expectations, and decrease cooperation expectations), and decrease rates of cooperation (secondary effect).

Second, it will test a compositional account of inequality, specifically that the unequal (vs. equal) group will have higher rates of stealing when there is a threshold (vs. not), i.e., primary effect, and that, as a consequence, this group will also have both worse expectations of what their partner will choose (i.e., higher stealing expectations, and lower cooperation expectations), and lower rates of cooperation, i.e., secondary effect. Importantly, across all conditions inequality will remain invisible (i.e., participants will not be informed about partner or other group members’ starting points level or current points level). 

To do this, the study will use a 2 X 2 design in which groups of players are randomly assigned to a Threshold condition (Threshold/No Threshold) and a Starting Points (Unequal/Equal) treatment condition. In the study, participants will play an interactive multiplayer game with the other members of their group. The goal for each participant in the game will be to accumulate as many points as possible because their points will determine the bonus payment they receive at the end of the experiment. 

Primary Predictions

The study’s primary predictions can be grouped by dependent variable: stealing, partner expectations (perceived likelihood that partner will steal, perceived likelihood that partner will cooperate), and cooperation. 

Stealing: 

We predict that players will be more likely to steal when they are below (vs. above) the threshold, and that players in the threshold-unequal condition will also be more likely to steal, i.e.: 

P1.1 Stealing will be more likely when a player’s points level is below (vs. above) the threshold (i.e., below 200 points in the threshold condition, and below 20 points in the no threshold condition), and 

P1.2 There will be an interaction between threshold and starting points conditions such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) conditions will be more likely to steal.

Partner Expectations: 

Next, we predict that being stolen from will negatively affect expectations of others, such that having been stolen from will lead to: 

P2.1 Higher expectations of partner stealing, and 

P2.2 Lower expectations of partner cooperation.  	

We also predict players in the threshold-unequal condition will have worse expectations of their partners. Specifically we predict that there will be an interaction between threshold and starting points conditions such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) conditions will report:

P3.1 Higher expectations of partner stealing, and 

P3.2 Lower expectations of partner cooperation. 

Note that if our partner expectation measures (of partner stealing, and of partner cooperation) are highly correlated (i.e., r >= 0.70), then we will generate an average measure of the two (see Variables and Analysis Plan below). In this case we predict: 

P2 Having been stolen from will lead to worse expectations of partners, and 

P3 There will be an interaction between threshold and starting points conditions such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) conditions will report worse expectations of their partner. 

Cooperation: 

We predict that having worse partner expectations will negatively impact cooperation, such that: 

P4.1 Participants with higher expectations of partner stealing will be less likely to cooperate, and 

P4.2 Participants with lower expectations of partner cooperation will be less likely to cooperate.  

Note again that if our expectations measures are highly correlated (i.e., r >= 0.70), then we will create a single average measure of partner expectations, in this case predict that:

P4 Participants with worse expectations of their partners will be less likely to cooperate. 

Last, we predict that players in the threshold-unequal condition will be the least likely to cooperate. Specifically we expect: 

P5 There will be an interaction between threshold and starting points conditions such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) conditions will be less likely to cooperate.

table.randomization:
Participants will be grouped by arrival time into groups of 8. The 8 members of each group will again be assigned the same group id. Groups will remain the same throughout the upcoming rounds. Each group will be assigned to one of four conditions, and we will vary the order of the 4 treatment assignments across groups, i.e., ‘unequal-threshold’, ‘equal-threshold’, ‘unequal-no-threshold’, ‘equal-no-threshold’.

At the beginning of each round, all 8 players in the group will enter a wait page while they are matched with another member of their group. To perform this matching the 8 participants with the same group id will be shuffled and four groups of size 2 will be formed.

Starting points will be assigned to participants using the corresponding distribution of each condition (i.e., {205} in equal condition and {180, 230} in unequal condition). We want to ensure similar mean and variance of starting resource distribution across multiple groups in the unequal conditions. Therefore, the starting points will be assigned as follows: after forming the groups of 8, we will assign 180 to four randomly chosen participants in the group and 230 to the remaining four participants.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will complete the study online, recruited from online psychology research platform Prolific (www.prolific.co). The study is implemented in oTree (Chen et al., 2016) and mounted on the Heroku webserver (www.heroku.com). The estimated time of the study is around 20-25 minutes, and the subjects will be paid on a rate of £9/hour plus the bonus payment they earn during the game.
table.sample_size: We determined our target sample size to be 512 participants, corresponding to approximately 64 groups (16 groups per treatment condition, with 8 participants per group), resulting in 128 participants per treatment condition.
table.sample_size_rationale: We arrived at this estimate by conducting a simulation-based power analysis using data from Study 4 of Radkani et al. (2023) to estimate the minimum sample size required to achieve 80% power (β = 0.80) to detect the interaction between the equality and threshold conditions. Specifically, we generated balanced sub-samples by randomly selecting participants in equal proportions from each treatment condition. For each candidate sample size (ranging from 160 to 544 in steps of 32), we ran 1,500 simulations, re-estimating the primary analysis of interest (P4.1), which tests for an interaction between threshold and equality conditions. For each sample size, we estimated power as the proportion of simulations in which the interaction term reached statistical significance at the 5% level.
table.stopping_rule:
Note that if participants drop out of the multiplayer game mid-game, they may be replaced by a bot such that the remaining participants can complete the survey. In this event additional groups may be conducted until we obtain the minimum required sample per condition.

Data collection will pause once the target sample size has completed the study. At this point, we will conduct our planned analysis and we also will run equivalence tests for our primary predictions to assess whether observed effects are meaningfully smaller than our smallest effect size of interest. For binary outcomes (e.g., whether a participant stole) we define this smallest effect size of interest as an odds ratio of 1.2, and for continuous outcomes we define it as a standardized mean difference of 0.2. table.manipulated_variables:
We will manipulate two variables. First, we will manipulate the level of inequality within groups (independent variable 1), i.e., whether all players in a group begin with 205 points (‘equal’ condition), or whether players begin the game evenly divided between 230 and 180 starting points (‘unequal’ condition). Note that in both conditions, the means of the two distributions are matched and equal to 205 points. 

Second, we will manipulate the desperation threshold level (independent variable 2), i.e., such that participants can reasonably expect to fall below it (threshold condition), or such that, while the threshold still exists, it is unlikely that participants will fall below (‘no threshold’ condition). In all four treatment conditions participants will lose their bonus payment if they end three consecutive rounds with a points level below the threshold. 

Both inequality and threshold variables will be manipulated between-groups, meaning that all 8 individuals in a group who interact with each other throughout the experiment will be assigned to the same inequality and threshold condition.
table.measured_variables: In each round, we will measure the decision of the participant (work alone, work together, steal) and their expectations about their partner’s choice, i.e., their rated likelihood that their partner will choose to work together, and their rated likelihood that their partner will choose to steal). Working together will be used as our measure of cooperative behaviour, and stealing will be used as our measure of antisocial behaviour. We will also measure whether or not a player has been stolen from in previous rounds, coded as 1 if the player has been stolen from in previous rounds, and as 0 if not. Last, we will measure a list of questions at the end of each round for exploratory analysis of player decision-making strategies and stealing perceptions.
table.indices: We will measure partner expectations using two variables (expected likelihood that partner will steal, and expected likelihood that partner will cooperate). If these measures are highly correlated (i.e., r >= 0.70), then we perform our analyses using an average measure of the two. To do this we will average the reverse coded expectations of partner stealing with expectations of partner cooperation to generate a single measure of partner expectations.
table.statistical_tests:
Across all confirmatory analyses: We will use mixed-effects models fitted with the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015), controlling for round number and accounting for the random effects of participant nested within group. For behavioral outcomes, we will model the likelihood of stealing (with ‘work together’ and ‘work alone’ coded as not-steal) and the likelihood of cooperation (with ‘steal’ and ‘work alone’ coded as not-cooperate). For expectation outcomes, we will model stealing expectations (i.e., rated likelihood of the partner stealing) and cooperation expectations (i.e., rated likelihood of the partner working together), or if they are highly correlated (i.e., r >= 0.70) we will model an average of the two. 

P1.1: We will model stealing behavior using a binomial distribution, with threshold status (above vs. below) included as a fixed effect. Our central prediction is that being below (vs. above) the threshold will be associated with a higher likelihood of stealing. The model will take the following form:

steal ~ threshold status + round + (1 | participant/group) 

P1.2: We will model stealing behavior using a binomial distribution, with equality condition, threshold condition, and their two-way interaction as fixed effects. Our central prediction is that the interaction will be significant such that participants in the unequal-threshold condition will have a higher likelihood of stealing. The model will take the following form:

steal ~ threshold condition * inequality condition + round + (1 | participant/group)

P2.1 & P2.2 (or P2): We will model partner expectations using a Gaussian distribution, with having been stolen from included as a fixed effect. Our central prediction is that having been stolen from (vs. not) will be associated with worse partner expectations (i.e., higher expectations of partner stealing, lower expectations of partner cooperation, or lower average partner expectations). The model(s) will take the following form:

If separate: 
expect_partner_steal ~ stolen_from + round + (1 | participant/group)
expect_partner_cooperate ~ stolen_from + round + (1 | participant/group)

If combined: 
expect_partner_avg ~ stolen_from + round + (1 | participant/group)

P3.1 & P3.2 (or P3): We will model partner expectations using a Gaussian distribution, with equality condition, threshold condition, and their two-way interaction as fixed effects. Our central prediction is that the interaction will be significant such that participants in the unequal-threshold condition have worse partner expectations (i.e., higher expectations of partner stealing, lower expectations of partner cooperation, or lower average partner expectations). The model(s) will take the following form:

If separate: 
expect_partner_steal ~ threshold condition * inequality condition + round + (1 | participant/group)
expect_partner_cooperate ~ threshold condition * inequality condition + round + (1 | participant/group)

If combined: 
expect_partern_avg ~ threshold condition * inequality condition + round + (1 | participant/group)

P4.1 & P4.2 (or P4): We will model cooperation behavior using a binomial distribution, with partner expectations (expected likelihood of stealing, cooperating, or an average) included as a fixed effect. Our central prediction is that having worse partner expectations (i.e., higher expectations of partner stealing, lower expectations of partner cooperation, or lower average partner expectations) will be associated with a lower likelihood of cooperating. The model will take the following form:

If separate: 
cooperate ~ expect_partner_steal + round + (1 | participant/group) 
cooperate ~ expect_partner_cooperate + round + (1 | participant/group) 

If combined: 
cooperate ~ expect_partern_avg + round + (1 | participant/group) 

P5: We will model cooperation behavior using a binomial distribution, with equality condition, threshold condition, and their two-way interaction as fixed effects. Our central prediction is that the interaction will be significant such that participants in the unequal-threshold condition will have a lower likelihood of cooperating. The model will take the following form:

cooperate ~ threshold condition * inequality condition + round + (1 | participant/group)
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p<0.05 criteria for determining if our results are significantly different from those expected if the null hypothesis were correct. We will conduct an F-test using Satterthwaite's approximation for the denominator degrees of freedom with the R package lmerTest to conduct a significance test of the fixed-effects parameters.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
As detailed in the Procedure section above, the decision and outcome pages have time limits. If a timeout happens on the decision page, the player’s choice will be replaced by that of a bot following the procedure as outlined in Study Design. We will only use data for participants replaced by a bots if they have played for at least 3 rounds prior to being replaced. Otherwise, we will exclude those players completely from our analyses. For players replaced by bots after more than 3 rounds, we will only analyze the decisions they made, not those made by the bot.

Last, we will include 4 mandatory comprehension questions that participants need to answer after reading the instructions. While we allow the participants to have multiple attempts, we count the number of errors they make for each question. We will perform robustness checks when restricting the dataset to participants with no or few errors.
table.exploratory_analyses:
In our exploratory analyses we will investigate three categories of question. First, we will test our hypothesized causal pathway between stealing, expectations, and cooperation, i.e., Do we observe a causal pathway between threshold status and stealing such that participants are more likely to steal when they are below the threshold, and does stealing, in turn, worsen partner expectations and decrease cooperation?

Second, we will explore the secondary effects of a compositional account of inequality specifically: Do people who have interacted with the people who are adversely affected perceive and behave differently?, i.e., What are the behavioural implications of navigating a world in which some people are desperate? Here we are interested in understanding how inequality affects everyone, not just those below the threshold, in ways that have important consequences for trust and for cooperation. Specifically we will examine if, in conditions with a threshold, participants above that threshold in the unequal (vs. equal condition) have worse expectations for their partner (i.e., expect less cooperation and more stealing), and if they themselves are less cooperative (i.e., cooperate less and steal more).

For both the first and second questions, we will restrict our analyses to the threshold conditions (i.e., exclude no threshold groups). This is because we are interested in investigating the effect of inequality, i.e., unequal (vs. equal) starting resources, in threshold groups on our four main dependent variables (stealing, expectations of partner stealing, expectations of partner working together, and working together). We will also test if our results change when accounting for the recency and frequency of stealing.

Third, across the full dataset, we will probe for the explanatory narratives participants give for: 
1) Their own decision-making strategy,
2) How they formed their expectations about what their partner would choose,
3) (If the participant was stolen from), why their partner stole, and
4) (If the participant stole), why they themselves stole.

table.title: Why does Inequality Reduce Trust and Undermine Cooperation? Testing the Role of Inequality Visibility
table.research_questions:
Research Question: Why does inequality reduce trust and undermine cooperation?  

It’s widely believed in social psychology and in other social science disciplines that inequality reduces trust and undermines cooperation. But it remains unclear why inequality would have this consequence. 

One way in which this might happen is via compositional effects, whereby the effects of inequality are reduced to the direct effects of what each individual has. This can have both primary effects, whereby people who are adversely affected by inequality behave differently, and secondary effects, whereby people who have interacted with the people who are adversely affected come to behave differently. These compositional effects can occur even when participants do not know about inequality. Another way in which the relationship between inequality, trust, and cooperation may be shaped is via inequality perceptions. Under this class of explanation, people perceive the inequality around them and have preferences for or psychological reactions to that inequality per se. This class of account predicts that inequality will affect trust because people are aware of it.

We experimentally test these accounts in the context of desperation thresholds, i.e., contexts in which there is a level of resources below which it is costly and potentially damaging to fall. Previous work uses desperation thresholds to help explain why inequality and deprivation produce high crime and low trust (see de Courson et al., 2025). This work predicts that people below a ‘desperation threshold’ should engage in risky behaviour (e.g., acquisitive crime) if doing so offers them the possibility of rapidly escaping above the threshold.

This study builds on an initial Study 1 in which we used a multiplayer experimental game to test for compositional effects of inequality on trust and cooperation (see https://osf.io/cwz7d/overview for study design and predictions). This study used a 2x2 experimental design varying the presence of a threshold and the starting levels of inequality among players. We found players were more likely to steal when their resource level fell below the desperation threshold. We also found more desperation in a group, by producing more stealing, reduced the group’s overall levels of trust and cooperation. Players in the unequal-threshold treatment had the highest levels of stealing, worst partner expectations and lowest levels of cooperation.

In the present study we will test the role played by inequality perceptions, i.e., does inequality have a greater impact on trust and cooperation when it is visible and, if so, what potential mechanisms could be driving those effects? This is motivated by an interdisciplinary literature which links economic inequality to trust and cooperation via inequality perceptions. This literature defines inequality in terms of disparity, specifically one’s relative position compared to relevant others (Mishra et al., 2015). Centering the role of social comparison (Festinger, 1954), these accounts propose that inequality affects downstream psychosocial and behavioural outcomes via various mechanisms such as status competition (Mishra et al., 2015; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2017; Willis et al., 2022), fairness perceptions (Buttrick & Oishi, 2017; Grosfeld & Senik, 2009; Smith et al. 2012; Willis et al., 2022), and negative affective responses to inequality (Dawes et al., 2007, Marmot, 2004; Sapolsky, 2005; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2009). Regardless of the proposed mechanisms at play, this literature is undergirded by the notion that perceptions of inequality matter: trust and cooperation should decrease when inequality is observable, interpretable, experienced as relevant to forecasting others’ intentions and/or as judged as unfair.

There are two important limitations to the inequality perceptions literature. First, it does not separate the effects of absolute resource scarcity from those of perceived relative disadvantage, making it impossible to disentangle the effects of perceived inequality from those of objective inequality alone. Second, it often leaves vague precisely how inequality is perceived. Much of the evidence relies on area-level inequality measures, implying that it is the experience of general inequality in one's environment (rather than interpersonal comparison with specific others) that matters. However other accounts argue that objective and subjective measures of inequality are often poorly correlated, at least in part, because people are more attuned to inequality in their daily lives, and that therefore inequality perceptions are formed via individual-level interactions rather than abstract-level knowledge of inequality in the population.

Present Study

In the present study we adapt Study 1’s paradigm to test the effects of inequality visibility on trust and cooperation in the context of desperation thresholds. In particular we will test how the visibility (vs. invisibility) of inequality affects trust and cooperation, and if this effect remains above and beyond inequality’s compositional effects.

To do this, the study will use a 2 X 2 X 3 design in which groups of players are randomly assigned to a threshold (threshold/no threshold), an inequality (unequal/equal starting points) and a visibility (invisible/visible-group/visible-partner) treatment. As in Study 1, participants will play an interactive multiplayer game with the other members of their group. The goal for each participant in the game will again be to accumulate as many points as possible because their points will determine the bonus payment they receive at the end of the experiment. The threshold and inequality treatments will be identical to those in Study 1. The invisible treatment will also be identical to that of Study 1, i.e., participants will be given no information about the points of the group or of their partner. In the visible-group treatment, in each round participants will be given information about the current points distribution among the other players in their group, although they will not be told the points level of the specific partner with whom they have been paired (i.e., they will have perfect information about the inequality within the group). In the visible-partner treatment, in each round participants will be given information about the current points of the partner with whom they have been paired, although they will not be told the points level of any other player in the group (i.e., they will have perfect information about the inequality between them and their partner). 

Research Question & Design Overview

Study 2 extends Study 1 by introducing a third experimental factor—inequality visibility, with three levels—while preserving the original 2X2 structure manipulating the presence of a desperation threshold (threshold vs. no threshold) and starting-point inequality (equal vs. unequal). The resulting 2X2X3 design allows us to examine how inequality, threshold constraints, and inequality jointly shape stealing behavior, partner expectations, and cooperation.

Primary Predictions

Our first set of predictions test if there are additive effects of visibility on our key outcome variables.

Outcome Variable: Stealing

P1 (Main effect of visibility): Stealing will differ between the invisible and visible conditions, averaged across threshold and inequality conditions.

P2 (Interaction with visibility): The effect of visibility on stealing will depend on the presence of a threshold, the level of inequality, or their combination.

Outcome Variable: Stealing Expectations

P3 (Main effect of visibility): Stealing expectations will differ between the invisible and visible conditions, averaged across threshold and inequality conditions.

P4 (Interaction with visibility): The effect of visibility on stealing expectations will depend on the presence of a threshold, the level of inequality, or their combination. 

Outcome Variable: Cooperation Expectations

P5 (Main effect of visibility): Cooperation expectations will differ between the invisible and visible conditions, averaged across threshold and inequality conditions.

P6 (Interaction with visibility): The effect of visibility on cooperation expectations will depend on the presence of a threshold, the level of inequality, or their combination. 

Outcome Variable: Cooperation

P7 (Main effect of visibility): Cooperation will differ between the invisible and visible conditions, averaged across threshold and inequality conditions.

P8 (Interaction with visibility): The effect of visibility on cooperation will depend on the presence of a threshold, the level of inequality, or their combination. 

Our second set of predictions concern replicating Study 1’s core results, i.e., for the outcome variables tested in Study 1. 

Outcome Variable: Stealing

P10 Stealing will be more likely when a player’s points level is below (vs. above) the threshold (i.e., below 200 points in the threshold treatment, and below 20 points in the no threshold treatment). 

P11 There will be an interaction between threshold and inequality such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) treatment groups will be more likely to steal.

Outcome Variable: Partner Expectations

Being stolen from will lead to: 

P12 Higher expectations that partners will steal, 

P13 Lower expectations that partners will cooperate.

There will be an interaction between the threshold and inequality treatments such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) treatment groups will report:

P14 Higher expectations that partners will steal, and 

P15 Lower expectations that partners will cooperate.

Outcome Variable: Cooperation

P16 Participants with higher expectations of partner stealing will be less likely to cooperate, 

P17 Participants with lower expectations of partner cooperation will be less likely to cooperate, and 

P18 There will be an interaction between threshold and inequality such that players in both the unequal (vs. equal) and threshold (vs. no threshold) treatments will be less likely to cooperate.

table.randomization:
Participants will be grouped by arrival time into groups of 8. The 8 members of each group will again be assigned the same group id. Groups will remain the same throughout the upcoming rounds. Each group will be assigned to one of 12 treatments, and we will vary the order of the 12 treatment assignments across groups.

At the beginning of each round, all 8 players in the group will enter a wait page while they are matched with another member of their group. To perform this matching the 8 participants with the same group id will be shuffled and four groups of size 2 will be formed.

Starting points will be assigned to participants using the corresponding distribution for each inequality treatment (i.e., {205} in equal treatment group and {180, 230} in unequal treatment group). We want to ensure similar mean and variance of starting resource distribution across multiple groups in the unequal treatment groups. Therefore, the starting points will be assigned as follows: after forming the groups of 8, we will assign 180 to four randomly chosen participants in the group and 230 to the remaining four participants.
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants will complete the study online, recruited from online psychology research platform Prolific (www.prolific.com). The study is implemented in oTree (Chen et al., 2016) and mounted on the Heroku webserver (www.heroku.com). The estimated time of the study is around 20-25 minutes, and the subjects will be paid on a rate of £9/hour plus the bonus payment they earn during the game.
table.sample_size: We determined our target sample size to be 1056 participants, corresponding to approximately 132 groups (11 groups per treatment, with 8 participants per group), resulting in 88 participants per treatment.
table.sample_size_rationale: We arrived at this estimate by conducting a simulation-based power analysis using data from Study 1 to estimate the minimum sample size required to achieve 80% power (β = 0.80) to detect the interactions between the inequality and threshold treatment groups. For each candidate sample size (ranging from 160 to 480 in steps of 32) and for each of our three predictions of interest (P2, P4, and P8), we ran 1,500 simulations, which tested for an interaction between threshold and equality treatment groups. For each sample size, we calculated empirical power as the proportion of simulations in which the interaction term reached statistical significance at the 5% level.

Importantly, across all conditions inequality will remain invisible (i.e., participants will not be informed about partner or other group members’ starting points level or current points level).

It’s widely believed in social psychology and in other social science disciplines that inequality reduces trust and undermines cooperation. But it remains unclear why inequality would have this consequence.

One way in which this might happen is via compositional effects, whereby the effects of inequality are reduced to the direct effects of what each individual has. This can have both primary effects, whereby people who are adversely affected by inequality behave differently, and secondary effects, whereby people who have interacted with the people who are adversely affected come to behave differently. These compositional effects can occur even when participants do not know about inequality. Another way in which the relationship between inequality, trust, and cooperation may be shaped is via inequality perceptions. Under this class of explanation, people perceive the inequality around them and have preferences for or psychological reactions to that inequality per se. This class of account predicts that inequality will affect trust because people are aware of it.

We experimentally test these accounts in the context of desperation thresholds, i.e., contexts in which there is a level of resources below which it is costly and potentially damaging to fall. Previous work uses desperation thresholds to help explain why inequality and deprivation produce high crime and low trust (see de Courson et al., 2025). This work predicts that people below a ‘desperation threshold’ should engage in risky behaviour (e.g., acquisitive crime) if doing so offers them the possibility of rapidly escaping above the threshold.

This study builds on an initial Study 1 in which we used a multiplayer experimental game to test for compositional effects of inequality on trust and cooperation (see https://osf.io/cwz7d/overview for study design and predictions). This study used a 2x2 experimental design varying the presence of a threshold and the starting levels of inequality among players. We found players were more likely to steal when their resource level fell below the desperation threshold. We also found more desperation in a group, by producing more stealing, reduced the group’s overall levels of trust and cooperation. Players in the unequal-threshold treatment had the highest levels of stealing, worst partner expectations and lowest levels of cooperation.

In the present study we will test the role played by inequality perceptions, i.e., does inequality have a greater impact on trust and cooperation when it is visible and, if so, what potential mechanisms could be driving those effects? This is motivated by an interdisciplinary literature which links economic inequality to trust and cooperation via inequality perceptions. This literature defines inequality in terms of disparity, specifically one’s relative position compared to relevant others (Mishra et al., 2015). Centering the role of social comparison (Festinger, 1954), these accounts propose that inequality affects downstream psychosocial and behavioural outcomes via various mechanisms such as status competition (Mishra et al., 2015; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2017; Willis et al., 2022), fairness perceptions (Buttrick & Oishi, 2017; Grosfeld & Senik, 2009; Smith et al. 2012; Willis et al., 2022), and negative affective responses to inequality (Dawes et al., 2007, Marmot, 2004; Sapolsky, 2005; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2009). Regardless of the proposed mechanisms at play, this literature is undergirded by the notion that perceptions of inequality matter: trust and cooperation should decrease when inequality is observable, interpretable, experienced as relevant to forecasting others’ intentions and/or as judged as unfair.

There are two important limitations to the inequality perceptions literature. First, it does not separate the effects of absolute resource scarcity from those of perceived relative disadvantage, making it impossible to disentangle the effects of perceived inequality from those of objective inequality alone. Second, it often leaves vague precisely how inequality is perceived. Much of the evidence relies on area-level inequality measures, implying that it is the experience of general inequality in one's environment (rather than interpersonal comparison with specific others) that matters. However other accounts argue that objective and subjective measures of inequality are often poorly correlated, at least in part, because people are more attuned to inequality in their daily lives, and that therefore inequality perceptions are formed via individual-level interactions rather than abstract-level knowledge of inequality in the population.

Present Study

In the present study we adapt Study 1’s paradigm to test the effects of inequality visibility on trust and cooperation in the context of desperation thresholds. In particular we will test how the visibility (vs. invisibility) of inequality affects trust and cooperation, and if this effect remains above and beyond inequality’s compositional effects.

To do this, the study will use a 2 X 2 X 3 design in which groups of players are randomly assigned to a threshold (threshold/no threshold), an inequality (unequal/equal starting points) and a visibility (invisible/visible-group/visible-partner) treatment. As in Study 1, participants will play an interactive multiplayer game with the other members of their group. The goal for each participant in the game will again be to accumulate as many points as possible because their points will determine the bonus payment they receive at the end of the experiment. The threshold and inequality treatments will be identical to those in Study 1. The invisible treatment will also be identical to that of Study 1, i.e., participants will be given no information about the points of the group or of their partner. In the visible-group treatment, in each round participants will be given information about the current points distribution among the other players in their group, although they will not be told the points level of the specific partner with whom they have been paired (i.e., they will have perfect information about the inequality within the group). In the visible-partner treatment, in each round participants will be given information about the current points of the partner with whom they have been paired, although they will not be told the points level of any other player in the group (i.e., they will have perfect information about the inequality between them and their partner).

Research Question & Design Overview

Study 2 extends Study 1 by introducing a third experimental factor—inequality visibility, with three levels—while preserving the original 2X2 structure manipulating the presence of a desperation threshold (threshold vs. no threshold) and starting-point inequality (equal vs. unequal). The resulting 2X2X3 design allows us to examine how inequality, threshold constraints, and inequality jointly shape stealing behavior, partner expectations, and cooperation.

If a timeout happens on the decision page, the player’s choice will be replaced by that of a bot following the procedure as outlined in Study Design. We will only use data for participants replaced by a bots if they have played for at least 3 rounds prior to being replaced. Otherwise, we will exclude those players completely from our analyses. For players replaced by bots after more than 3 rounds, we will only analyze the decisions they made, not those made by the bot. We will replace groups with more than 2 players who time out (i.e., who do not complete the game for reasons other than falling below the threshold and being converted into a bot).

Last, we will include 4 mandatory comprehension questions that participants need to answer after reading the instructions. While we allow the participants to have multiple attempts, we count the number of errors they make for each question. We will perform robustness checks and may restrict the dataset to participants with no or few errors.", "In our exploratory analyses we will investigate four categories of question. The first three of these questions parallel the exploratory analyses conducted in Study 1. The final of these questions will probe for potential psychological mechanisms at play.
First, we will test our hypothesized causal pathway between stealing, expectations, and cooperation, i.e., Do we observe a causal pathway between threshold status and stealing such that participants are more likely to steal when they are below the threshold, and does stealing, in turn, worsen partner expectations and decrease cooperation?

Second, we will explore secondary effects, specifically: Do people who have interacted with the people who are adversely affected perceive and behave differently? Specifically we will examine if, in treatments with a threshold, participants above that threshold in the unequal (vs. equal treatment) have worse expectations for their partner (i.e., expect less cooperation and more stealing), and if they themselves are less cooperative (i.e., cooperate less and steal more).

For both the first and second questions, we will again restrict our analyses to the threshold treatment groups (i.e., exclude no threshold groups).

Third, across the full dataset, we will again probe for the explanatory narratives participants give for:

1) Their own decision-making strategy,
2) How they formed their expectations about what their partner would choose,
3) (If the participant was stolen from), why their partner stole, and
4) (If the participant stole), why they themselves stole.

Last, to probe for potential psychological mechanisms at play we will test whether our six self-reported ratings (negative emotions during the game, negative emotions towards other players, zero-sum mindset, competitiveness, fairness perceptions of the game, and fairness perceptions towards other players) vary by condition using a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). Restricting the sample to participants in the Threshold condition who were above the threshold (n = 2,927 rounds, 392 participants, 66 groups), inequality in the form of unequal starting points predicted worse partner expectations: participants in Unequal groups expected more stealing, b = 0.49, 95% CI [0.05, 0.92], p = .030, and expected less cooperation, b = -0.47, 95% CI [-0.95, 0.01], p = .053.

Restricting the sample to participants in the Threshold condition who were above the threshold (n = 2,927 rounds, 392 participants, 66 groups), inequality in the form of unequal starting points predicted worse partner expectations: participants in Unequal groups expected more stealing, b = 0.49, 95% CI [0.05, 0.92], p = .030, and expected less cooperation, b = -0.47, 95% CI [-0.95, 0.01], p = .053.

However, although the results were directionally consistent with study 1, Unequal starting points did not significantly predict above-threshold participants' own behavior: stealing, OR = 1.37, 95% CI [0.82, 2.30], p = .224, and cooperation, OR = 0.65, 95% CI [0.36, 1.21], p = .174, did not differ significantly between Equal and Unequal groups.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05"), Text = c("We generated balanced sub-samples for each candidate sample size (160 to 544, in steps of 32), ran 1,500 simulations per candidate size, and calculated empirical power as the proportion of simulations in which the interaction reached significance at p < .05.", "Empirical power at a given sample size was estimated as the proportion of simulations in which that interaction reached significance at p < .05." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including 'README' in the name of your overview document.

#### Archive Files

The following files are not ZIP archives: threshold.otreezip.gz, threshold2.otreezip.gz, my_test_package-1.0-py3.7.egg. We recommend the `.zip` format for archives: only ZIP stores its file listing in a way that lets a tool inspect the contents without downloading the whole archive, so a `.zip` is more discoverable and re-usable than a `.7z`, `.rar`, `.tar` or `.tar.gz`.

#### Registration's Source Project Is Closed

1 OSF source project is closed. The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration's own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project's access setting. Nothing is currently lost, but this is still worth fixing: a closed source project means the files only survive for as long as the registration's copy does, and anyone who follows the project link itself (rather than the registration) will find it inaccessible.

- **https://osf.io/2xje3** is closed; its files were retrieved from the OSF registration https://osf.io/qw4a7/overview, https://osf.io/qw4a7.

Consider making the source project openly available.

#### Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository's files are grouped: the manuscript names a study (ex4) with no matching files in the repository. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 15192 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: compiled Python files (3765), editor settings (6), operating system (10981), R history (1), version control (439). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

live_data_statements: It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others' points, knew their partner's points, or knew the group's point distribution.
In each round participants were randomly paired with three other members of their microsociety.
Participants were adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via the online research platform Prolific.
The study took approximately 15-20 minutes, and participants were paid at a rate of £9 per hour plus the bonus payment earned during the game.
Participants completed the experiment in groups of eight, with each group assigned to one of the four conditions.

The Threshold treatment determined the points level below which participants were penalised: 200 points in the Threshold conditions (a level below which participants could reasonably expect to fall) and 20 points in the No Threshold conditions (a level low enough that falling below was extremely unlikely to occur, which still preserved a formal penalty structure and equivalent complexity of instructions).
Participants completed eight rounds of the game.
In each round, participants were randomly paired with another member of their group, yielding four partner pairs.
After choosing and reporting what they expected their partner to choose, participants were shown their own choice, their partner's choice, and how their own points had changed (or remained the same).
Throughout, participants were shown a visual of their own points level relative to the threshold and the number of strikes they had incurred.

Follow-up simple contrasts found that, within the Threshold treatment level, Unequal participants had significantly greater odds of stealing than Equal participants, OR = 6.92, 95% CI [3.31, 14.49], z = 5.14, p < .001.

Crucially, we observed inequality's effects-more stealing, lower trust, less cooperation-without inequality ever being perceived, since no participant ever knew how many points any other participant had.
Participants were again adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific.

In study 1, participants were substantially more likely to steal when their resources fell below the desperation threshold (primary effect), participants who had been stolen from trusted subsequent partners less, and this mistrust in turn predicted participants' own cooperation (secondary effect).
Participants had no information about the resource levels of others, demonstrating that inequality can increase crime, reduce trust, and lower cooperation even when it is entirely unobserved.

We also tested the additional effect of inequality visibility by adding two conditions; one in which participants were informed of the resource level of their partner, one in which they were informed of the distribution of resources in the group.

This shortfall was due to 42 participant-level timeouts spread across all twelve treatment cells (range 1-7 per cell; largest shortfall in the equal, No-Threshold, Visible-Partner cell), consistent with the pre-registered stopping rule under which timed-out participants are replaced by a bot for the remainder of the session rather than the group being re-run.
Participants replaced by bots no longer had control over their in-game choices, were directed to return the study on Prolific, and were still paid a show-up fee.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 843 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified

124 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others' points, knew their partner's points, or knew the group's point distribution.
In each round participants were randomly paired with three other members of their microsociety.
Participants were adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via the online research platform Prolific.
The study took approximately 15-20 minutes, and participants were paid at a rate of £9 per hour plus the bonus payment earned during the game.
Participants completed the experiment in groups of eight, with each group assigned to one of the four conditions.

The Threshold treatment determined the points level below which participants were penalised: 200 points in the Threshold conditions (a level below which participants could reasonably expect to fall) and 20 points in the No Threshold conditions (a level low enough that falling below was extremely unlikely to occur, which still preserved a formal penalty structure and equivalent complexity of instructions).
Participants completed eight rounds of the game.
In each round, participants were randomly paired with another member of their group, yielding four partner pairs.
After choosing and reporting what they expected their partner to choose, participants were shown their own choice, their partner's choice, and how their own points had changed (or remained the same).
Throughout, participants were shown a visual of their own points level relative to the threshold and the number of strikes they had incurred.

Follow-up simple contrasts found that, within the Threshold treatment level, Unequal participants had significantly greater odds of stealing than Equal participants, OR = 6.92, 95% CI [3.31, 14.49], z = 5.14, p < .001.

Crucially, we observed inequality's effects-more stealing, lower trust, less cooperation-without inequality ever being perceived, since no participant ever knew how many points any other participant had.
Participants were again adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific.

In study 1, participants were substantially more likely to steal when their resources fell below the desperation threshold (primary effect), participants who had been stolen from trusted subsequent partners less, and this mistrust in turn predicted participants' own cooperation (secondary effect).
Participants had no information about the resource levels of others, demonstrating that inequality can increase crime, reduce trust, and lower cooperation even when it is entirely unobserved.

We also tested the additional effect of inequality visibility by adding two conditions; one in which participants were informed of the resource level of their partner, one in which they were informed of the distribution of resources in the group.

This shortfall was due to 42 participant-level timeouts spread across all twelve treatment cells (range 1-7 per cell; largest shortfall in the equal, No-Threshold, Visible-Partner cell), consistent with the pre-registered stopping rule under which timed-out participants are replaced by a bot for the remainder of the session rather than the group being re-run.
Participants replaced by bots no longer had control over their in-game choices, were directed to return the study on Prolific, and were still paid a show-up fee.
