text.text: Higher inequality is associated with higher crime, lower trust, and lower cooperation, but the mechanisms producing these associations remain unclear.
Inequality produces compositional effects through changing individuals' resource levels, regardless of whether or not it is perceived.
Inequality's visibility may have further effects precisely because people perceive it.
In Study 1 (N = 496; 64 groups), participants played a multiplayer experimental game in groups of eight, choosing to steal from one another, cooperate, or work alone.
Participants' were never informed of others' points levels.

Inequality in the initial points distribution increased stealing rates, lowered trust, and reduced the rate of cooperation, but only when there was a points threshold below which it was disastrous to fall.
Study 2 (N = 1,014; 132 groups) replicated these findings.
It also tested the additional role of visibility by varying whether participants had no information about others' points, knew their partner's points, or knew the group's point distribution.
Making inequality visible had no meaningful effect on any outcome.

Together, these findings provide evidence for compositional, but not visibility, effects of inequality: distributing resources unequally around a threshold increased crime, reduced trust, and lowered cooperation, whether or not inequality was visible.

Populations with higher levels of inequality have more antisocial behaviour (Kelly, 2000; Kennedy et al., 1998; Rufrancos & Power, 2013), lower trust (Algan & Cahuc, 2013; Barone & Mocetti, 2016; Buttrick & Oishi, 2017; Rothstein & Uslaner, 2005), and less cooperation (Alesina & La Ferrara, 2000; Bolaños et al., 2021; Lancee & Van De Werfhorst, 2012).
text.formatted: Populations with higher levels of inequality have more antisocial behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kelly, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kennedy et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Rufrancos & Power, 2013)</ref>, lower trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Algan & Cahuc, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barone & Mocetti, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Buttrick & Oishi, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Rothstein & Uslaner, 2005)</ref>, and less cooperation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alesina & La Ferrara, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Bolaños et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lancee & Van De Werfhorst, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The micro-level processes through which these associations are produced remain unclear.

This is, in part, because the effects of inequality as a statistical property-how resources are distributed in a population such that more inequality exacerbates the material constraint of those at the bottom-are rarely teased apart from inequality's effects as a social phenomenon, which people perceive and react to.

At a minimum, increasing inequality might increase crime, reduce trust and undermine cooperation through its compositional effects, wherein the change in aggregate behaviour is a simple consequence of the change in the level of resources that each individual has (Gravelle, 1998; Nettle & Dickins, 2026).
text.formatted: At a minimum, increasing inequality might increase crime, reduce trust and undermine cooperation through its compositional effects, wherein the change in aggregate behaviour is a simple consequence of the change in the level of resources that each individual has <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gravelle, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Nettle & Dickins, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When a resource distribution becomes more dispersed without changing its mean, the tails of the distribution are pushed towards the extremes, leaving more people at the bottom end with a very low level of material resources.

This produces primary effects, whereby people at the bottom of the distribution find themselves in difficult circumstances and behave differently (e.g., engage in more acquisitive crime); and secondary effects, whereby people exposed to this behaviour in turn alter their own behaviour (e.g., become less trusting because they have been stolen from).
Compositional effects rely only on people's reaction to their own material conditions, and exposure to the behaviour of others in the population.
They do not require anyone to perceive the dispersion of resources, or have any particular attitude towards inequality per se.
Compositional effects may be particularly strong in contexts with desperation thresholds: levels of resources below which it is disastrous to fall.

This insight comes from the desperation threshold model (DTM; De Courson & Nettle, 2021; de Courson et al., 2025) which proposes that utility declines steeply below a threshold at which basic needs are no longer met.
text.formatted: This insight comes from the desperation threshold model <ref type="bibr">(DTM;</ref> <ref type="bibr">De Courson & Nettle, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">de Courson et al., 2025)</ref> which proposes that utility declines steeply below a threshold at which basic needs are no longer met.

text.text: People just above the threshold should be risk-averse, seeking to avoid falling below it, whereas people just below the threshold should be more willing to take risks that offer a possibility of returning above it.
Holding average resources constant, increasing inequality pushes a larger proportion of the population below the threshold.

Those below the threshold engage in more risk-taking and acquisitive behaviour (a primary effect), which in turn reduces trust and cooperation among people who have been stolen from even if they themselves have never been below the threshold (a secondary effect).
Thus, higher levels of inequality should lead to more crime, lower levels of trust, and less cooperation even when inequality is invisible.

Said another way, in societies where desperation thresholds exist, inequality imposes harsh material constraints on those at the bottom, and these constraints not only incentivise anti-social behaviour in those at the bottom, but also reduce the trust and cooperation of everyone in society through interactions with those people. Radkani et al. (2023) tested these predictions using an experimental paradigm in which participants earned "energy points" that were converted into bonus payments, with a penalty deducted for each round in which their earnings fell below a specified threshold.
text.formatted: Said another way, in societies where desperation thresholds exist, inequality imposes harsh material constraints on those at the bottom, and these constraints not only incentivise anti-social behaviour in those at the bottom, but also reduce the trust and cooperation of everyone in society through interactions with those people. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al. (2023)</ref> tested these predictions using an experimental paradigm in which participants earned "energy points" that were converted into bonus payments, with a penalty deducted for each round in which their earnings fell below a specified threshold.

text.text: Participants played in "microsocieties" of eight.
In each round participants were randomly paired with three other members of their microsociety.
They then chose to work alone, cooperate with the other players for a small potential gain, or steal from them for a larger potential gain but also a risk of losing points if they were caught.
In study 4 the authors tested a compositional account of inequality, predicting that inequality's effects would uniquely exist when there was both a desperation threshold and inequality.

They did this using a 2x2 design which manipulated both the presence of a desperation threshold and the degree of resource inequality among players, thereby testing whether greater inequality produces more stealing and, in turn, lower trust and cooperation. Radkani et al.'s (2023) findings were largely consistent with the predictions of the DTM: players were more likely to steal when their resource level fell below the desperation threshold.
text.formatted: They did this using a 2x2 design which manipulated both the presence of a desperation threshold and the degree of resource inequality among players, thereby testing whether greater inequality produces more stealing and, in turn, lower trust and cooperation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> findings were largely consistent with the predictions of the DTM: players were more likely to steal when their resource level fell below the desperation threshold.

text.text: Moreover, greater desperation in a group, by producing more stealing, reduced that group's overall trust and cooperation, suggesting that the consequences of desperation extended beyond those directly experiencing it.
The present study is motivated by several methodological limitations of Radkani et al. (2023).
text.formatted: The present study is motivated by several methodological limitations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: In study 4, inequality in the threshold conditions increased stealing in early rounds, but not overall, perhaps because differences in actual inequality between the conditions attenuated over rounds.
They also did not find significant differences in trust or cooperation, despite unequal groups stealing more in early rounds.

The first objective of the present research was to replicate the main findings of Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4 using an improved game and a more effective manipulation of inequality. Radkani et al.'s (2023) paradigm was limited to testing compositional effects.
text.formatted: The first objective of the present research was to replicate the main findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study 4 using an improved game and a more effective manipulation of inequality. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> paradigm was limited to testing compositional effects.

text.text: However, some scholars assert that inequality visibility may provide another important avenue through which inequality shapes trust and cooperation.

They propose that perceived inequality affects behaviour through a variety of psychological mechanisms (e.g., status competition and zero-sum beliefs, Davidai, 2025; Mishra et al., 2015; Sánchez-Rodríguez et al., 2019; Sommet & Elliot, 2023; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2017; Willis et al., 2022; fairness perceptions, Buttrick & Oishi, 2017; Grosfeld & Senik, 2009; Smith et al., 2012; Willis et al., 2022; and negative affective responses to inequality, Dawes et al., 2007; Marmot, 2004; Sapolsky, 2005; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2009).
text.formatted: They propose that perceived inequality affects behaviour through a variety of psychological mechanisms (e.g., status competition and zero-sum beliefs, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Davidai, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Mishra et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Sánchez-Rodríguez et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sommet & Elliot, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Wilkinson & Pickett, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Willis et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">fairness perceptions, Buttrick & Oishi, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Grosfeld & Senik, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Smith et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Willis et al., 2022</ref>; and negative affective responses to inequality, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dawes et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Marmot, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Sapolsky, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Wilkinson & Pickett, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Regardless of the specific mechanism proposed, these accounts share the premise that inequality's effects depend on its perception: inequality should affect crime, trust, and cooperation precisely because disparities are observable, and because people have a psychological response to the magnitude of those disparities or to their own relative standing.
Though visibility effects are plausible, epidemiological evidence conflates the effects of visible inequality with those of absolute material constraint.

Moreover, different dimensions of inequality visibility (e.g., awareness of the population-level resource distribution versus disparities compared to specific interaction partners) may shape trust and behavior in distinct ways.
The second objective of the present study was to investigate how inequality visibility shapes antisocial behaviour, trust and cooperation.

In Study 2, we extended Radkani et al.'s (2023) paradigm to introduce conditions with group-level visibility (awareness of the population-wide resource distribution), and dyadic visibility (awareness of resource disparities with a specific interaction partner).
text.formatted: In Study 2, we extended <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> paradigm to introduce conditions with group-level visibility (awareness of the population-wide resource distribution), and dyadic visibility (awareness of resource disparities with a specific interaction partner).

text.text: This design allowed us to isolate the effects of inequality visibility from the compositional effects of inequality, and to test whether group-level and dyadic visibility independently shaped stealing, trust and cooperation.
Study 1 aimed to test a purely compositional account of inequality's effects, replicating and improving Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4.
text.formatted: Study 1 aimed to test a purely compositional account of inequality's effects, replicating and improving <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study 4.

text.text: We predicted that Unequal (vs.

Equal) groups would have higher rates of stealing when a threshold existed below which participants could reasonably expect to fall, that these Unequal-Threshold groups would also have lower levels of trust (in the form of worse expectations of their partner), and lower levels of cooperation.

We also predicted that we would recover the intermediate behavioural effects observed in Radkani et al.'s (2023) study: participants below (vs. above) the desperation threshold would steal more; exposure to stealing would worsen participants' expectations of what their partner would choose to do (increasing stealing expectations and decreasing cooperation expectations) and decrease rates of cooperation (see Table 3 for full list of pre-registered predictions).
text.formatted: We also predicted that we would recover the intermediate behavioural effects observed in <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study: participants below (vs. above) the desperation threshold would steal more; exposure to stealing would worsen participants' expectations of what their partner would choose to do (increasing stealing expectations and decreasing cooperation expectations) and decrease rates of cooperation (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> for full list of pre-registered predictions).

text.text: This experimental paradigm improved three limitations of Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4.
text.formatted: This experimental paradigm improved three limitations of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study 4.

text.text: In their study, first, the differences in players' points levels between the unequal and equal conditions attenuated over time.
We modified the parameters so that the Inequality treatment had a more pronounced difference in starting levels of inequality.

Second, the rules of the game were relatively complicated in ways that may have been difficult for players to understand-in particular, the threshold penalty (a deduction from the bonus payment applied only at the end of the game, based on the cumulative number of below-threshold rounds) may have been unintuitive, and because choices were made in groups of four, the potential outcomes may have been opaque.
We simplified the rules by pairing players in dyads rather than in groups of four.
Third, applying threshold penalty deductions only at the end of the experiment meant players may not have fully experienced the consequences of falling below the threshold during play.

We implemented a more intuitive "strikes-based" threshold penalty system in which players lose their bonus if they end three consecutive rounds below the threshold, making the consequences of falling below more salient during play rather than only at the end.
For more detail, see the Supplementary Materials S1.
Participants were adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via the online research platform Prolific.
We determined our target sample size via a simulation-based power analysis targeting 80% power (β = .80) to detect the Threshold × Starting Points interaction.
This was based on Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4 and determined to be 512 participants (approximately 64 groups of 8, 16 groups per treatment condition, 128 participants per condition).
text.formatted: This was based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study 4 and determined to be 512 participants (approximately 64 groups of 8, 16 groups per treatment condition, 128 participants per condition).

text.text: The final sample for Study 1, after exclusions, included 496 participants and 3,661 observations (64 groups; M age = 42.6, SD = 13.0, range = 18-81; 53% female, 46% male, 1% unreported).
The study took approximately 15-20 minutes, and participants were paid at a rate of £9 per hour plus the bonus payment earned during the game.
Data collection was paused once the target sample size had completed the study.
As pre-registered, participants who dropped out mid-game were replaced by bots, and additional groups were run as needed to reach the minimum required sample per condition.
Participants who either ended three consecutive rounds below the threshold or who failed to respond within the choice-page time limit were replaced by bots in subsequent rounds.
Bots followed a choice protocol designed to approximate the participant's prior choices when possible, and to select Work Alone when not.
Bots made 307 of all choice decisions (7.7%), and these decisions were excluded from analyses.
Participants' choices were included if they chose in at least three rounds; for participants replaced before three rounds, both their choices and all subsequent bot choices were excluded.
See Supplementary Materials S2, for more detail.
The experiment was implemented in oTree (Chen et al., 2016) and hosted on the Heroku webserver (www.heroku.com).

text.text: Prior to running the experiment, we first ran a simulation to confirm that, given our experimental design and parameters, players would have an incentive to steal when they fell below the threshold (see Supplementary Materials S3).
text.formatted: Prior to running the experiment, we first ran a simulation to confirm that, given our experimental design and parameters, players would have an incentive to steal when they fell below the threshold (see Supplementary Materials <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>).

text.text: The experiment had a 2 (Threshold: No Threshold vs.
Threshold) × 2 (Inequality: Equal vs.
Unequal Starting Points) design.
Participants completed the experiment in groups of eight, with each group assigned to one of the four conditions.

The Threshold treatment determined the points level below which participants were penalised: 200 points in the Threshold conditions (a level below which participants could reasonably expect to fall) and 20 points in the No Threshold conditions (a level low enough that falling below was extremely unlikely to occur, which still preserved a formal penalty structure and equivalent complexity of instructions).

The Inequality treatment manipulated inequality in starting points while holding mean starting points constant: in the Equal conditions, all eight participants received 205 starting points, whereas in the Unequal conditions, four randomly selected participants received 180 points and the remaining four received 230 points.
See Table 1 for experimental parameters.
text.formatted: See Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for experimental parameters.

text.text: Participants completed eight rounds of the game.
In each round, participants were randomly paired with another member of their group, yielding four partner pairs.
Participants then chose to steal, work together, or work alone, and reported how likely they thought their partner was to steal and to cooperate.
Stealing was the riskiest option, resulting in a large gain if successful and a larger loss if caught, with a 50% chance of being caught.
Cooperation (working together) was less risky, resulting in a small gain if their partner also worked together, and a small loss if their partner tried to steal and was successful.
If either or both partners chose to work alone, both partners' points level remained unchanged and there was no risk (see Table 2).
text.formatted: If either or both partners chose to work alone, both partners' points level remained unchanged and there was no risk (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The desperation threshold was operationalised using a strikes-based system.

Players received a strike for each round ended below the threshold; if a player accumulated three strikes the game ended and they lost their bonus payment, but if they ended a round at or above the threshold prior to receiving three strikes in a row, their strike counter reset to zero.
After choosing and reporting what they expected their partner to choose, participants were shown their own choice, their partner's choice, and how their own points had changed (or remained the same).
Throughout, participants were shown a visual of their own points level relative to the threshold and the number of strikes they had incurred.
They were given no information about their partner's identity or points level (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: They were given no information about their partner's identity or points level (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Note.
Example choice page for round 1 for participant in the Threshold-Equal condition, with the participant's current points level (205) and threshold (200, red line) displayed.
The strikes indicator shows the participant has no strikes.
We analyzed four outcome variables.
Two were binary choice outcomes: steal, coded 1 when participants chose to steal and 0 otherwise, and cooperate, coded 1 when participants chose to work together and 0 otherwise.
Given the existence of a third option (Work alone), these can be considered as independent outcomes (the correlation between stealing and cooperating was r = -.56 in study 1 and r = -.52 in study 2).
We measured trust in two ways: stealing expectations, for which higher values indicated less trust, and cooperation expectations, for which higher values indicated greater trust.
Both were measured on 10-point scales which asked how likely participants thought their partner was to steal or to work together, respectively (1 = extremely unlikely,10 = extremely likely).
As preregistered, we analyzed these expectation measures separately because they were not strongly correlated (Study 1: r = -.42; Study 2: r = -.37).
We also derived a 'stolen from' indicator, coded 1 if a partner had been stolen from in a previous round.
We analyzed behavioral outcomes using logistic mixed-effects models and expectation outcomes using linear mixed-effects models.
Models were fitted in R using the lme4 and lmerTest packages (Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Models were fitted in R using the lme4 and lmerTest packages <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bates et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: All models included a centered round variable to account for linear changes across rounds and random intercepts for participant and group.
We used α = .05 throughout, and all confidence intervals reported are Wald intervals.
Each prediction was tested with its own mixed-effects model.
Five predictions (P1.1, P2.1, P2.2, P4.1, and P4.2) tested a single directional main effect.
The remaining four predictions (P1.2, P3.1, P3.2, and P5) tested Threshold × Inequality interactions.

As well as null hypothesis significance tests, we carried out equivalence testing using two one-sided tests (TOST) with the pre-registered region of practical equivalence of an odds ratio of 0.833-1.2 for the binary outcomes (stealing, cooperation) and a standardised mean difference of ±0.2 for the continuous expectation ratings (reported in Supplementary Materials S4).
Tests of pre-registered predictions are reported in Table 3.

text.text: Study 1 replicated and expanded upon the core findings of Radkani et al.'s (2023) study 4 using an improved design.
text.formatted: Study 1 replicated and expanded upon the core findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al.'s (2023)</ref> study 4 using an improved design.

text.text: In the presence of a binding minimum resource threshold, an unequal distribution of resources in the microsociety led to increased stealing, lower trust in the form of higher partner stealing expectations and lower partner cooperation expectations, and less cooperation.

Among groups where there was a resource threshold, the presence of inequality sharply raised stealing (P1.2) and the expectation of being stolen from (P3.1), though not the expectation of cooperation (P3.2).
It also lowered cooperation (P5).
Among groups with no resource threshold, the same Inequality manipulation had no discernable effect on expectations or cooperation.
Partner expectations closely tracked and predicted behavior.
Being stolen from worsened expectations in terms of both more expected stealing (P2.1), and less expected cooperation (P2.2).

Those expectations were, in turn, strong predictors of cooperative choice: higher stealing expectations predicted less cooperation (P4.1), while higher cooperation expectations predicted more cooperation (P4.2).
Exploratory analysis also supports Radkani et al. (2023)'s finding that inequality's effects were not confined to participants below the threshold.
text.formatted: Exploratory analysis also supports <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Radkani et al. (2023)</ref>'s finding that inequality's effects were not confined to participants below the threshold.

text.text: Restricting the sample to participants in the Threshold treatment level above the threshold (n = 1,471 rounds, 193 participants, 32 groups), participants in Unequal groups expected more stealing, b = 0.84, 95% CI [0.22, 1.46], p = .009, expected less cooperation, b = -0.85, 95% CI [-1.47, -0.22], p = .010, stole more themselves, OR = 2.76, 95% CI [1.27, 6.03], p = .011, and cooperated less, OR = 0.16, 95% CI [0.06, 0.46], p = .001 than participants in Equal groups.
This suggests the effects of inequality on behavior and expectations are not solely a function of being below the threshold-they persist even among participants above it.

Crucially, we observed inequality's effects-more stealing, lower trust, less cooperation-without inequality ever being perceived, since no participant ever knew how many points any other participant had.

Study 2 built on study 1, asking additionally whether inequality has a further effect on stealing, trust and cooperation when it is visible and, if so, how visibility of group-level inequality differs from visibility of dyadic inequality.
We did this by crossing study 1's original 2 (Threshold: Threshold vs.
No Threshold) × 2 (Inequality: Unequal vs.
Equal Starting Points) design with a third factor, Visibility, which had three levels.
In the Invisible conditions, as in study 1, participants received no information about any other player's resource level.
In the Visible-Group conditions, participants saw the resource distribution of the whole group at every choice occasion (without identifying which player was their current partner).

In the Visible-Partner conditions, participants saw their current partner's resource level at each choice occasion, without being given knowledge about the overall distribution of resources within the group.
The Threshold and Inequality manipulations were unchanged from study 1 (for choice pages by visibility treatment level and a list of deviations from study 1 see Supplementary Materials S6 and S7).
We had primary predictions for Study 2 concerning Visibility (see Table 4), as well as replication predictions of the effects seen in Study 1 (Table 3).
text.formatted: We had primary predictions for Study 2 concerning Visibility (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>), as well as replication predictions of the effects seen in Study 1 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: We predicted that stealing, trust (in the form of partner expectations), and cooperation would differ across the three visibility conditions.

For each outcome we predicted a main effect of Visibility, averaged across Threshold and Inequality (P1, P3, P5, P7), and that the effect of Visibility would depend on Threshold, Inequality, or their combination (P2, P4, P6, P8).

As for replication predictions, we predicted more stealing below the desperation threshold, especially in Unequal groups (P10-P11); that being stolen from would worsen expectations of a new partner's behaviour (P12-P15); and that these expectations would predict cooperation, with lowest cooperation in the Threshold-Unequal condition (P16-P18).
Participants were again adults residing in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific.
We determined our target sample size via a simulation-based power analysis using data from study 1, targeting 80% power (β = .80) to detect the Threshold × Starting Points interaction.
This was determined to be 1,056 participants (approximately 132 groups of eight, 88 participants per treatment cell).
The final sample for Study 2, after exclusions, included 1,014 participants and 7,419 observations (132 groups; M age = 38.9, SD = 12.4, range = 18-84; 58% female, 40% male, 2% unreported).
The same data collection and bot replacement rules were implemented as used in study 1.
Bots made 693 of all choice decisions (8.5%), and again all analyses excluded these decisions.
Categorical predictors were effects-coded, so that lower-order effects represent averages across the levels of the other factors and interactions represent deviations from additive effects.
All primary models included a Threshold × Starting Points × Visibility interaction term.

To enable comparability with study 1, for the replication predictions (P10-P18), the replication results reported in Table 3 matched the model specifications for each corresponding prediction in study 1, using the same treatment contrast coding and without including the Visibility variable in the model.

text.text: Study 1's results were replicated.

Stealing was significantly more likely when players were below (vs. above) the threshold (Table 3, P10; Figure 3a), and was also significantly higher in the Threshold-Unequal condition (Table 3, P11; Figure 3b); planned contrasts confirmed inequality increased stealing within Threshold groups, OR = 3.85, 95% CI [2.49, 5.95], z = 6.06, p < .001, but not within No-Threshold groups, OR = 1.29, 95% CI [0.85, 1.98], z = 1.19, p = .233.

text.text: Restricting the sample to participants in the Threshold condition who were above the threshold (n = 2,927 rounds, 392 participants, 66 groups), inequality in the form of unequal starting points predicted worse partner expectations: participants in Unequal groups expected more stealing, b = 0.49, 95% CI [0.05, 0.92], p = .030, and expected less cooperation, b = -0.47, 95% CI [-0.95, 0.01], p = .053.

However, although the results were directionally consistent with study 1, Unequal starting points did not significantly predict above-threshold participants' own behavior: stealing, OR = 1.37, 95% CI [0.82, 2.30], p = .224, and cooperation, OR = 0.65, 95% CI [0.36, 1.21], p = .174, did not differ significantly between Equal and Unequal groups.
Two key findings emerged from these analyses.
First, the compositional effects observed in study 1 replicated with only one exception.
Notably, stealing (P11) and stealing expectations (P14) were both higher when there was both a binding threshold and unequal starting resources.
This effect was concentrated almost entirely within the Threshold treatment level: Unequal Starting Points raised stealing and stealing expectations only when a threshold was present.

Cooperation expectations (P15) and cooperation itself (P18) showed the same pattern and, when decomposed, a significant simple effect within the Threshold condition, though neither Threshold x Inequality interaction was significant.
Being stolen from raised expectations that a new partner would steal and lowered expectations that they would cooperate (P12, P13).
Those expectations were, in turn, strong predictors of cooperative choice: higher stealing expectations reduced cooperation (P16), and higher cooperation expectations raised it (P17).

Exploratory analysis which restricted the sample to participants above the threshold partially supported Study 1's finding that the effects of inequality extend to those above the threshold; participants above the threshold had lower trust in their partner in the form of higher stealing expectations and lower cooperation expectations.
However, while directionally consistent, the results on the behaviour of those above the threshold were not statistically significant.
Second, we found little meaningful evidence for an effect of inequality visibility.

None of the four additive effects of visibility were significant (P1, P3, P5, P7), and of the twelve visibility-interaction terms tested (P2, P4, P6, P8), only one reached significance: Inequality × Visibility on cooperation (P8).

While follow-up contrasts located this effect specifically in the Group-Visibility condition, the broader pattern remained that making inequality visible, either in the form of knowing the distribution of points in the group or in knowing an interaction partner's points level, had little detectable effect on any outcome.
In two microsociety experiments, we investigated why greater inequality could lead to more stealing, lower trust and less cooperation.
We studied this question in the context of desperation thresholds, a minimum level of resources below which it is costly to fall.

We first allowed for purely compositional effects produced through people's reaction to their own resource levels and to the behaviour of others; then, in study 2, we examined the additional effects of people being aware of inequality through the visibility of other's resources.
Across two studies, we found consistent evidence for compositional effects, but little evidence that making inequality visible had any additional effect on stealing, trust or cooperation.

In study 1, participants were substantially more likely to steal when their resources fell below the desperation threshold (primary effect), participants who had been stolen from trusted subsequent partners less, and this mistrust in turn predicted participants' own cooperation (secondary effect).
Inequality increased stealing and reduced trust, but only where there was also a desperation threshold.

Exploratory analyses further suggested that inequality's effects extended beyond those directly experiencing material constraint: even among participants above the threshold, those in unequal groups stole more, trusted their partner less, and cooperated less.
Participants had no information about the resource levels of others, demonstrating that inequality can increase crime, reduce trust, and lower cooperation even when it is entirely unobserved.
In study 2 we replicated these compositional effects.

We also tested the additional effect of inequality visibility by adding two conditions; one in which participants were informed of the resource level of their partner, one in which they were informed of the distribution of resources in the group.
Neither had a meaningful effect on stealing, trust, or cooperation.
We used an experimental microsocieties paradigm to generate these findings.
While this methodological approach enables us to tease apart inequality's compositional and visibility effects, it does not allow us to capture the full richness of real-world social processes.

Rather than viewing this as a weakness, we view this as a strength: even in a brief, abstract, and low-stakes context where the consequences of falling below the threshold are minimal, participants still stole, trusted each other less, and cooperated less when both inequality and a desperation threshold were present.
We did not find that inequality has the same effects on stealing, trust and cooperation in the absence of a threshold.
However, we believe desperation thresholds are widespread.

People's valuations of material resources are typically S-shaped, with very steep welfare gains where extra resources allow people to meet basic needs (Kapteyn & Wansbeek, 1985; Nettle & Wolff, 2025).

text.text: For example, despite living in one of the world's largest economies (Alston, 2018), one in five people in the United Kingdom experienced poverty in 2022/23, where one in four of those in poverty (3.5 million people) was food insecure (Joseph Rowntree Foundation, 2026).

text.text: As such, it is reasonable to expect that desperation thresholds are relevant even in high income populations because there are still people in those contexts who cannot meet important basic needs.

Taken together these findings suggest that, when a desperation threshold exists below which it is possible to fall, an unequal distribution of resources alone is sufficient to generate higher crime, reduced trust, and lower cooperation; these effects occur whether or not inequality is visible.
We do not interpret these findings to mean that there is no real-world effect of inequality visibility on societal outcomes.

Rather we interpret them in terms of the causal potency of inequality: in contexts with desperation thresholds, inequality can produce behavioural and psychological effects, even when no one knows what anyone else has.
We thus interpret these findings to imply that inequality matters under many circumstances.

Inequality's effects-increased crime, reduced trust, and reduced cooperation-harm both individuals and societies (Alesina & La Ferrara, 2000; Algan & Cahuc, 2013; Buttrick & Oishi, 2017; Kelly, 2000; Wilkinson & Pickett, 2017).

text.text: We generated balanced sub-samples for each candidate sample size (160 to 544, in steps of 32), ran 1,500 simulations per candidate size, and calculated empirical power as the proportion of simulations in which the interaction reached significance at p < .05.

text.text: From our initial sample, one group had more than 2 dropouts (3 players who timed out during gameplay); as pre-registered, this group was dropped and replaced with a new group, leaving 512 participants across 64 groups (16 groups per treatment condition).
All remaining groups had 2 or fewer players who dropped before round 3.
We then excluded participants who completed fewer than 3 rounds of gameplay, leaving 498 participants across 64 groups, and removed all bot-generated observations.
This left a final analytic sample of 496 participants across 64 groups (16 groups per treatment condition), or 3,661 round-level observations.
We determined our target sample size of 1,056 participants (approximately 132 groups of eight, 88 participants per treatment cell) via a simulation-based power analysis using data from Study 1.

For each candidate sample size, ranging from 160 to 480 in steps of 32, and for each of our three focal interaction predictions (P2, P4, P8), we generated 1,500 simulated balanced sub-samples and tested for a significant Threshold × Unequal Starting Points interaction in each.
Empirical power at a given sample size was estimated as the proportion of simulations in which that interaction reached significance at p < .05.
text.formatted: Empirical power at a given sample size was estimated as the proportion of simulations in which that interaction reached significance at p < .05.

text.text: We selected the smallest candidate sample size giving at least 80% power across these three predictions and scaled it up to the full 2 × 2 × 3 design.

The achieved sample reached the group-level target exactly-132 groups-but fell 42 participants short of the participant-level target: 1,014 participants across those 132 groups (7,419 round-level choices after exclusions), or 96.0% of the 1,056 target.

This shortfall was due to 42 participant-level timeouts spread across all twelve treatment cells (range 1-7 per cell; largest shortfall in the equal, No-Threshold, Visible-Partner cell), consistent with the pre-registered stopping rule under which timed-out participants are replaced by a bot for the remainder of the session rather than the group being re-run.
As in Study 1, participants who dropped out mid-game were replaced by a bot for the remainder of the session, and data collection was set to pause once the target sample size was reached.

Following this stopping rule, all 132 target groups were completed; the achieved participant-level shortfall (1,014 of 1,056) reflects timeouts that occurred late enough in a group's session, or distributed enough across it, that re-running the group was judged unnecessary rather than a departure from the pre-registered rule.
The achieved analytic sample after these exclusions was 1,014 participants across 132 groups (7,419 round-level observations).
Choice pages carried a 1.5-minute time limit and outcome pages a 2-minute time limit in all rounds; once the limit elapsed, pages were submitted automatically.
A participant who did not respond on the choice page was replaced by a bot for the rest of the experiment, so that the remaining active participants could finish the game.
Bots submitted "NA" on the expectation sliders.

A bot replacing a participant who had completed at least 3 rounds chose stochastically, matching the probabilities of that participant's own choices up to the point of replacement (e.g., a participant who chose work alone, work together, and steal once each across 3 rounds would be replaced by a bot with a ⅓ probability of choosing each option).
A bot replacing a participant with fewer than 3 completed rounds instead matched the choice probabilities of the group's other active players in the immediately preceding round.
Bots also automatically submitted the outcome page.
Participants replaced by bots no longer had control over their in-game choices, were directed to return the study on Prolific, and were still paid a show-up fee.
A participant who ended three consecutive rounds below the threshold and lost their bonus likewise had all subsequent choice pages submitted automatically by a bot.

text.text: As described above, the main difference from Study 1 was the addition of a third manipulated factor visibility.
There were two further, minor procedural differences.
First, the bonus payment in study 2 was calculated at a rate of 0.5 pence per point (versus 1 pence per point in study 1).
Average bonus payment among participants who received a bonus were £2.23 (min £1.25, max £2.75) in study 1 and £1.09 (min £0.68, max £1.45) in study 2.

Second, after the eighth and final round, participants additionally rated six items probing potential psychological mechanisms-negative emotions during the game, negative emotions toward other players, a zero-sum mindset, competitiveness toward other players, fairness perceptions of the game, and fairness perceptions toward other players-before reporting their age and gender and being debriefed.
These ratings were collected for exploratory use and are not reported here.

text.text: We shifted rounds from an interaction in groups of 4 players to dyadic interaction between partners.

We replaced the No Threshold condition in which no threshold exists with a No Threshold condition in which, while the threshold still exists, it is set at such a low level that the risk of falling below it is negligible.

This makes the experimental instructions more similar between conditions, and helps rule out the alternative explanation that behavioural differences between conditions result from the mere existence of a threshold rather than from being below or at risk of falling below it.

We replaced starting levels in the unequal condition-previously drawn evenly from the set {180, 190, 220, 230}-with starting levels drawn from the set {180, 230}, reducing the risk of attenuation across rounds and aiding parsimony, since our hypotheses concern being above or below a threshold rather than degree of inequality.

We replaced Radkani et al.'s (2023) threshold penalty (20 pence deducted per round ended below the threshold) with a strikes-based penalty rule whereby players lose their bonus if they end three consecutive rounds below the threshold, making the penalty more intuitive and better ensuring players experience it during play.

created a Shiny app in R (code available on OSF: https://osf.io/e6rs5/files/osfstorage) simulating a series of choices (repetitions = 500, rounds = 8) in which agents hold "points" each round and accumulate "bonus points" across rounds.

Agents started with one of four points levels-{-20, -15, 15, 20}-expressed relative to a desperation threshold level set to 0 (the multiplayer experiment itself sets the threshold at a positive value, e.g., 200 points).

The outcome of each round depended on both the agent's choice and a hypothetical partner's choice (set with some probability to steal, cooperate, or work alone), with payoff parameters mirroringRadkani et al. (2023): 5 points for mutual cooperation, -5 points for a cooperator whose partner stole successfully, 0 points for a cooperator whose partner's theft failed, 10 points for a successful theft, and -15 points for a failed theft attempt (50% success probability).
